column3: Angels surrounding the Throne praise their Lord, directly supplying the focus scene's attendant circle.
Divine choosing, teaching, and completing favor do not clarify the angels' intercession or protection from Hell.
Believers ask their Lord for forgiveness and protection from the Fire, closely matching the focus prayer's two requests.
Angels praise their Lord and seek forgiveness for those on earth, the closest parallel to the focus's interceding angels.
It names divine signs, provision, and turning back, but adds little to the focus prayer.
The marriage prohibitions and closing divine mercy do not illuminate the focus.
God's mercy encompasses everything and is assigned to the God-fearing believers, clarifying the focus's appeal to all-encompassing mercy.
The inability of false gods to help is a distant contrast to the focus's plea for divine protection.
Faithful God-consciousness until death broadly supports the focus's address to believers, without its intercessory content.
Sincere repentance, forgiveness, and a believers' prayer for completion connect repentance to divine protection.
The immediate continuation explicitly asks protection from evils and calls that protection mercy.
It directly joins repentance, seeking forgiveness, and divine mercy, though it adds less than the fuller prayers already listed.
A group of servants says, "Our Lord, we believe; forgive us and have mercy," providing a collective prayer parallel.
The lack of intercessors is a contrast that marks the focus's angelic plea as dependent on God's acceptance.
Mary carrying her child does not clarify bearing the Throne or intercession.
Believers respond to faith with a communal request for forgiveness and removal of sins.
The nearby warning that no intercessor is obeyed for wrongdoers bounds the focus prayer for repentant believers.
It explicitly says that eight bear the Throne of the Lord, directly clarifying the focus's Throne-bearers.
Believers prostrate and praise their Lord without pride, paralleling the focus's praise and faith.
The absence of an intimate friend reinforces the final helplessness from which the focus seeks protection.
Noah is carried on the ark, offering only a general contrast to the Throne-bearers' carrying role.
It denies that deceivers can carry another's sins, usefully distinguishing responsibility from the focus's benevolent intercession.
Disputing God's signs does not add to the focus prayer.
The names Most Merciful and Especially Merciful ground the focus's appeal to mercy, but without its intercessory action.
Regular praise of the Lord by day and night parallels the focus's praise formula.
Kind speech when unable to give is not a substantive parallel to the focus.
God is worthy both of reverent caution and forgiveness, joining avoidance of harm with pardon.
The command to praise the Lord and seek His forgiveness exactly joins the two devotional acts in the focus.
The condemned confess sins and seek a way out, but it does not clarify the believers' prayer.
God is named Lord of the mighty Throne, clarifying the sovereignty of the Throne borne in the focus.
Its communal closing prayer joins burdens, pardon, forgiveness, mercy, and aid, strongly expanding the focus's protective petition.
Forgetting God and self-forgetfulness do not illuminate the focus's angelic intercession.
God is Lord of the Throne and uniquely sovereign, giving theological context for the Throne scene.
God protects the righteous from the punishment of Hell, directly naming the outcome sought in the focus.
The immediate continuation asks that the believers and their righteous families be admitted to the promised gardens.
Warning believers to fear the Fire only generally relates to the focus's request for protection from it.
Faith and holding fast to God lead into mercy and a straight path, paralleling believers following God's way.
The loss of mutual support before the Fire gives a distant contrast to the focus's requested protection.
The Forgiving, Merciful Lord delays deserved punishment, showing mercy as compatible with judgment.
Those who do wrong, then repent and believe, meet a Forgiving, Merciful Lord, matching the focus conditions.
The chains and dragging of the condemned give a concrete contrast to the requested protection from Hell.
The blessing and ingratitude of Sheba do not materially clarify the focus.
Those who commit evil, then repent and reform, find their Lord Forgiving and Merciful.
The final reward of the truthful gives a broad eschatological outcome, without the focus's prayer or protection.
Believers are told to confer for righteousness and God-consciousness, a limited communal parallel.
Moses confesses wrongdoing and receives forgiveness, showing the personal form of the pardon sought for believers.
No one can protect people from God on that day, sharply framing the focus's request for His protection.
God carries people in the ark through overwhelming waters, a remote carrying-and-preservation parallel.
Moses' prayer against Pharaoh's wealth and faith does not illuminate the focus intercession.
God admits believing righteous people into His mercy, supplying the promised result of the focus prayer.
Jacob promises to seek his Lord's forgiveness for his sons, a direct human example of intercession.
God encompasses all things in knowledge, closely echoing the focus's appeal to encompassing mercy and knowledge.
Travel by livestock and ships uses carrying language but does not explain the Throne-bearers.
God-consciousness is presented as a way to receive mercy, broadly related to the focus's appeal for believers.
Addressing those around Pharaoh does not illuminate the focus's attendants around the Throne.
Envy over worldly favor does not clarify the focus.
The Mighty Forgiver governs the ordered cosmos, providing only a broad backdrop for mercy and sovereignty.
The account of 'Ad's rejection and disobedience does not add to the focus.
Each soul is repaid without injustice on the day of reckoning, supplying the judgment setting for the prayer's protection.
Perseverance, mutual steadfastness, and God-consciousness offer only a general model of believers' conduct.
Repentance, prayer, and almsgiving lead to release under divine forgiveness and mercy, but the setting is distinct.
Signs in rain, revival, and changing winds do not materially illuminate the focus prayer.
The direct command to seek God's forgiveness is a concise parallel to the angels' request.
Moses asks, "forgive us and have mercy on us," a collective supplication closely related to the focus.
It joins patience with seeking forgiveness and praising the Lord morning and evening, directly echoing the focus's praise and forgiveness.
Noah's grateful descendants being carried do not clarify the focus's intercession.
Following the messenger removes burdens and fetters, a limited parallel to relief from the burdens of sin.
Testing whether the hoopoe speaks truth does not illuminate the focus.
Bringing a queen's throne is only a distant literal parallel to bearing the divine Throne.
Angels glorify God night and day without weariness, complementing the focus's praising angelic company.
God's knowledge of hidden glances and hearts does not add to the focus's stated mercy and knowledge.
Believers who do good receive forgiveness and generous provision, a concise statement of the hoped-for outcome.
Mountains and birds glorify God with David, a non-angelic but related praise scene.
The warning against obeying disbelievers does not clarify the focus.
False gods cannot intercede or save from harm, a contrast to seeking God's protection.
The Merciful is established over the Throne, directly joining divine mercy and Throne sovereignty.
The believer's warning to Pharaoh about divine might does not clarify the focus prayer.
Cooperation in righteousness and God-consciousness supplies only a broad communal ethic.
The righteous are protected from the punishment of Hell, directly realizing the focus's request.
God pardons believers after their retreat, a limited instance of forgiveness after failure.
Moses asks forgiveness for himself and his brother and entry into mercy, a close collective-prayer parallel.
Hearts sealed for following desires do not clarify the focus.
God promises support to messengers and believers, broadly supporting the focus's concern for believers.
The youths ask their Lord for mercy and rightly directed affairs, a direct supplicatory parallel.
The ordered courses of night, day, sun, and moon form only a remote cosmic context.
Judgment by revelation and the consequences of turning away offer a distant contrast to following God's way.
The Merciful is established upon the Throne, directly relating mercy to the Throne named in the focus.
The hypothetical gods would seek a way to the Lord of the Throne, affirming His unique authority.
The Lord's forgiveness is vast for those avoiding major sins, closely supporting the focus's appeal to expansive mercy.
Naming God as Lord of the mighty Throne offers limited sovereignty context.
Judging by truth and not following desire broadly relates to following God's way and avoiding punishment.
The Lord of heavens and earth is the Mighty Forgiver, joining universal sovereignty with forgiveness.
The account of sorcery and its harm does not clarify the focus.
Mercy provides a warning to people lacking a prior warner, showing mercy as guidance before judgment.
Disbelievers' comparison of status and assemblies does not illuminate the focus.
Turning to the Merciful Lord in trust offers a limited parallel to returning and following God's way.
Inheritance shares and familial benefit do not clarify the focus.
It denies that any force can help apart from the Merciful, a contrast that underscores dependence on God.
The command to repent collectively gives only a distant connection to the focus's repentant believers.
The God-conscious are in shade and springs, a broad image of the protected outcome sought in the focus.
A communal prayer asks for good in both lives and direct protection from the punishment of the Fire.
Believers ask their Lord not to let their hearts deviate and to grant mercy from Himself.
A faithful community asks for forgiveness of sins, excess in its affairs, firmness, and victory.
Wrongdoers are forgiven when they repent to God and the Messenger seeks forgiveness for them, an explicit intercessory parallel.
One who wrongs himself and then seeks God's forgiveness finds Him Forgiving and Merciful.
Jesus entrusts the guilty to God and acknowledges that forgiveness belongs to His sovereign wisdom.
Those who do wrong ignorantly and then repent and reform meet a Forgiving, Merciful Lord.
Adam and his wife jointly confess wrongdoing and ask for forgiveness and mercy to avoid loss.
Seeking forgiveness is named as a condition preventing divine punishment.
The Messenger's prayers are described as a source of tranquility for believers, a related intercessory care.
Seeking forgiveness and repenting to God are joined to divine provision and favor.
Abraham asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, and the believers on the Day of Reckoning.
God declares forgiveness for those who repent, believe, do righteousness, and remain rightly guided.
The prayer, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy," closely matches the focus's collective appeal to divine mercy.
Servants ask their Lord to avert from them the punishment of Hell, directly paralleling the focus's final petition.
Repentance, faith, and righteous deeds lead God to transform evil deeds, emphasizing mercy after return.
God and His angels care for believers by bringing them from darkness into light, an angelic-believer parallel.
God's servants are told not to despair of His all-encompassing forgiveness.
God commands people to call upon Him and promises an answer, grounding the focus's petitionary form.
Angels descend upon steadfast believers with reassurance against fear and grief.
Angels declare themselves allies of believers in this life and the Hereafter, closely extending the focus's angelic care.
God accepts repentance from His servants, pardons evil deeds, and knows what they do.
Answering God's caller brings forgiveness of sins and protection from a painful punishment.
The Messenger is commanded to seek forgiveness for believing men and women, a direct counterpart to the focus's intercession.
Believing men and women are admitted to gardens and their evil deeds are removed.
The reverent seek forgiveness before dawn, adding a devotional setting for repentance.
Believers pray for completed light and forgiveness on the Day their light runs before them.
Later believers pray, "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith," a close communal intercession.
Faith and striving bring forgiveness of sins and admission to gardens.
On the Day of Gathering, God removes the evil deeds of believers and admits them to gardens.
Noah calls his people to seek their Lord's forgiveness, for He is ever forgiving.
Noah asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, everyone entering his house as a believer, and all believing men and women.
God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day and grants brightness and joy.
